Triggers.value: Difficulty breathing or feeling short of breath

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Talking with others about the event or its aftermath
Open or exposed spaces where I feel vulnerable

Threat.value: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing
The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me

Negative Appraisals.value: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it
The people responsible have faced no consequences
The event happened because of the way I acted

issues.item: Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body
issues.explanation: 'Body Shame' is difficult to reconcile with the rest of the profile for a civilian-in-war-zone trauma unless there is some indication of bodily violation, injury, or humiliation. The other selected items center on injustice, impunity, hypervigilance, dissociative/fragmented memory, and avoidance, but provide no supporting context for body-focused shame, making this item stand out as clinically mismatched.

issues.item: Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
issues.explanation: The Threat items emphasize pervasive current danger and hypervigilance (scanning exits, needing to stay alert at night), but the formulation specifically has Triggers → Threat inactive. In this profile, Triggers are concrete reminders such as car sounds and related media, yet the Threat items are generalized and not plausibly linked to those triggers; this makes the threat presentation feel disconnected from the trigger pattern.

vignette: At 74 years old, Rajit found himself living a life overshadowed by memories of a violent past that haunted him in ways he could not escape. As a welder, he had always been proud of his craftsmanship and the way he provided for his family, but after surviving a war as a civilian in his home country, the sounds of a car engine or the rumble of tires on pavement could send him spiraling into a panic. These auditory triggers brought back vivid images of the chaos and the fear he felt during those dark days, punctuating his life in America with an unsettling breathlessness. In response to these overwhelming auditory reminders, Rajit found himself steering conversations away from any mention of the war, believing that by doing so, he would protect himself from the painful memories that threatened to engulf him. Whenever he heard a car approaching, he felt an overwhelming tightness in his chest, as though the memories themselves were suffocating him. To cope, he often found himself redirecting his thoughts to mundane tasks, unwilling to engage with the memories that felt too raw and painful to confront. Rajit’s memories were fragmented, often feeling alien to him, as if they belonged to someone else. He grappled with the dissonance of recalling horrifying details while also feeling like he was piecing together a puzzle with missing pieces. This incomplete picture only fueled his sense of injustice; it seemed profoundly unfair that he had endured such trauma, and he felt that no one was held accountable for the suffering inflicted upon innocent lives like his. The anger and sense of betrayal bred a belief that he was somehow to blame for his fate, a thought that further exacerbated his reluctance to share his experiences. This belief solidified his decision to avoid discussing his past, convincing him that any attempt to open up would only lead to further pain and judgment, further isolating him from those who cared about him. Talking about the war, he felt, would only invite judgment or pity, so he avoided those conversations altogether, reinforcing a cycle of isolation that left him feeling even more disconnected from the world around him. As the years passed, Rajit noticed that he was becoming increasingly vigilant. Night after night, he lay awake, straining to hear the slightest sound, convinced that remaining alert would somehow protect him from the horrors he had witnessed. His heightened state of awareness extended into his waking life, where he had difficulty concentrating on tasks at work, often finding himself lost in thought or distracted by the echoes of past trauma. This constant sense of threat made even mundane experiences, like the rush of traffic outside, feel charged with danger, and he found himself flinching at the sound of engines, each one a reminder of the chaos he had tried so hard to escape. Each day, he navigated through life’s demands while grappling with an internal storm, where the weight of his memories collided with an ever-present sense of threat. He felt vulnerable in open spaces, convinced they could expose him to danger, prompting him to seek refuge in familiar, enclosed areas where he felt a semblance of safety. Rajit’s memories, though fragmented, were persistent and powerful. He learned that if he kept himself busy at work, he could drown out the intrusive memories that threatened to surface, leading him to take on more projects than he could handle, just to avoid being alone with his thoughts. "The urgency of those memories would flood his mind with a sense of threat, compelling him to withdraw from conversations or avoid discussions about current events, as he feared they would reawaken the trauma he struggled to manage." They served as constant reminders of the violence he had experienced, triggering feelings of helplessness and despair. "This constant sense of threat heightened his sensitivity to everyday sounds, making him perceive even mundane noises as potential triggers that could bring forth painful memories." "His belief that danger lurked around every corner heightened his sensitivity to everyday sounds, making him hyper-aware of potential triggers that could bring forth painful memories." The more he tried to dismiss these memories, the more they seemed to call out to him, weaving themselves into his daily life. "This visceral reaction prompted him to take longer routes to work, avoiding busy streets altogether, as he believed steering clear of those auditory triggers would protect him from the onslaught of painful memories." When he encountered media coverage of war or violence, the visceral reactions they evoked left him feeling as if he were reliving those moments all over again. "This constant state of alertness was a response to the auditory triggers that sent him into a spiral of panic; he believed that by being vigilant, he could somehow shield himself from the painful memories that lurked just beneath the surface." "Once those memories broke through, they filled him with a sense of threat, making him feel as if danger was still lurking just beneath the surface, preventing him from fully engaging with his work or colleagues." Each report fed into his feelings of injustice, further entrenching his belief that he had not only been a victim of circumstances but also a victim of societal indifference, where no acknowledgment of his suffering existed. "These memories, once they surfaced, brought with them an overwhelming sense of threat, making Rajit feel as though the danger he had faced was not just a thing of the past but something that could return at any moment." In this seemingly endless loop, Rajit’s maladaptive strategies became ingrained. "Rajit's conviction that his experiences would only invite pity or misunderstanding kept him silent, reinforcing his maladaptive strategy of evasion and avoidance in conversations with loved ones." He found himself avoiding discussions about his past, redirecting conversations to safe topics, and steering clear of situations that could trigger unwelcome memories. "Rajit recognized that his avoidance of social interactions and discussions about his past not only pushed people away but also confirmed his negative appraisal that he was unworthy of connection and understanding." Each time he did this, he believed he was protecting himself, yet a part of him recognized the toll it was taking on his relationships. "This avoidance of confronting his memories only served to keep them alive and potent, as each time he sidestepped the pain, he felt the memories grow stronger, echoing in his mind with a renewed urgency." vignette_attempts.vignette: At 74 years old, Rajit found himself living a life overshadowed by memories of a violent past that haunted him in ways he could not escape. As a welder, he had always been proud of his craftsmanship and the way he provided for his family, but after surviving a war as a civilian in his home country, the sounds of a car engine or the rumble of tires on pavement could send him spiraling into a panic. These auditory triggers brought back vivid images of the chaos and the fear he felt during those dark days, punctuating his life in America with an unsettling breathlessness. In response to these overwhelming auditory reminders, Rajit found himself steering conversations away from any mention of the war, believing that by doing so, he would protect himself from the painful memories that threatened to engulf him. Whenever he heard a car approaching, he felt an overwhelming tightness in his chest, as though the memories themselves were suffocating him. To cope, he often found himself redirecting his thoughts to mundane tasks, unwilling to engage with the memories that felt too raw and painful to confront. Rajit’s memories were fragmented, often feeling alien to him, as if they belonged to someone else. He grappled with the dissonance of recalling horrifying details while also feeling like he was piecing together a puzzle with missing pieces. This incomplete picture only fueled his sense of injustice; it seemed profoundly unfair that he had endured such trauma, and he felt that no one was held accountable for the suffering inflicted upon innocent lives like his. The anger and sense of betrayal bred a belief that he was somehow to blame for his fate, a thought that further exacerbated his reluctance to share his experiences. This belief solidified his decision to avoid discussing his past, convincing him that any attempt to open up would only lead to further pain and judgment, further isolating him from those who cared about him. Talking about the war, he felt, would only invite judgment or pity, so he avoided those conversations altogether, reinforcing a cycle of isolation that left him feeling even more disconnected from the world around him.
